en: The Diamond Sutra of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Supreme Mahāyāna Teaching of the Southern School,
in One Scroll: The Dharma Platform Sutra Expounded by the Sixth Patriarch,
Master Huineng, at the Dafan Temple in Shaozhou.

The Record Compiled by Dharma-Heir Fa Hai, Part One: Bestowing the Formless Precepts. Master Huineng ascended the high seat in the lecture hall of the Dafan Temple and preached the Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, bestowing the formless precepts upon his disciples who propagate the Dharma.

At that time, more than ten thousand monastics and laypeople, both clergy and laity, seated in the assembly—including over thirty officials led by Wei Ju, the Prefect of Shaozhou, and over thirty Confucian scholars—jointly requested the Great Master to expound the Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

The Provincial Governor then ordered his disciple, the monk Fahai, to compile this record for circulation among future generations. May those who study the Way uphold this fundamental principle, transmitting it to one another so that they may have something to rely upon and follow as their inheritance; thus he preached this *Platform Sutra*.
In the second act, National Teacher Neng said:
"Good friends!
With a pure mind, recite the Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
The Great Master remained silent for a while, purifying his mind and spirit, before finally speaking:
"Good friends, listen attentively:
my compassionate father’s original official post was in Fanyang; he was demoted and exiled to Lingnan, where he became a commoner in Xinzhou."
When I, Huineng, was young, my father also passed away early.
Left orphaned by my aged mother, we moved to Nanhai.
Enduring hardship and poverty, I sold firewood in the marketplace.
Suddenly, a guest came to buy firewood, so he led Huineng to the government store; the guest took the wood away.
Having received the money, Huineng returned to the gate and suddenly saw another guest reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon hearing this once, Huineng’s mind became clear and he attained enlightenment.
He then asked the guest,
"From where have you come, and why do you carry this scripture?"

The guest replied, "I have been to Fengmao Mountain east of Huangmei County in Qizhou to pay my respects to the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren; he is currently there, with more than a thousand disciples."

I heard from him that the Great Master exhorted both monastics and laypeople that by merely upholding a single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one immediately realizes one's nature and directly attains Buddhahood.

Upon hearing these words, Huineng realized that his past karma had created a karmic affinity; he immediately took leave of his kin and traveled to Fengmao Mountain at Huangmei to pay homage to the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren.
The third section: Master Hongren asked Huineng, "From what region do you come?
Why have you come to this mountain to pay homage to me? What is it that you seek from me now?"
Huìnéng replied, "I am a native of Lingnan, a commoner from Xīnzhōu. I have come from afar specifically to pay my respects to the Master; I seek nothing else, but only to become a Buddha."
The Master then rebuked Huineng, saying, "You are a man from Lingnan, and moreover a hunter; how can you possibly become a Buddha?
Huineng replied:
"Human beings have north and south, but the Buddha-nature has neither north nor south;
although the bodies of the hunters and the monk are different, how could there be any difference in their Buddha-nature?"
The Master wished to speak further with him, but seeing those around him standing by his side, he remained silent; he then dismissed Huineng, ordering him to join the assembly in their labors.
At that time, there was a practitioner who assigned Huineng to the mortar house to tread the pestle for over eight months.
On the fourth day, the Fifth Patriarch suddenly summoned all his disciples; once they had assembled, he called them together.
The Fifth Patriarch said,
"I have told you that for people of the world, the matter of birth and death is of great importance.
You disciples spend all day making offerings, seeking only fields of merit, yet do not seek to escape the bitter sea of birth and death."
"You are deluded regarding your own nature; how can the gates of merit save you?
Return to your rooms for now and examine yourselves. Those who possess wisdom should personally realize the *prajñā* of their original nature and each compose a verse to present to me."
"I have examined your verse; if you have realized its great meaning, I shall entrust to you the robe and the Dharma to be transmitted as the sixth generation.
Act with urgency!
Upon receiving these instructions, the fifth-generation disciple returned to his respective quarters and said to one another:
“We have no need to clarify our minds or exert ourselves to compose verses to present to the Master.
The Venerable Shenxiu is our preceptor; once the Venerable Xi has attained the Dharma, we shall naturally rely upon him, so there is no need to compose verses!”
The people stilled their minds, and none dared to present a verse.

At that time, there were three bays of corridor in front of the Master’s hall; offerings were made beneath this corridor, and he intended to paint the *Laṅkāvatāra* transformation scenes, as well as the lineage of the Five Patriarchs transmitting the Dharma-robes and the teaching for posterity as a record.
The painter Lu Zhen examined the wall and began his work the following day.
On the sixth day, the head monk Shenxiu reflected:

"Since the others have not yet presented their mind-verses, and as I am the teacher-instructor, if I do not present my own mind-verse, how will the Fifth Patriarch be able to see the depth or shallowness of my understanding?"

"I shall present my verse on the mind to the Fifth Patriarch to express my intent; it would be well if I seek the Dharma, but it would not be well if I merely seek the patriarchate. To do so would be to act with an ordinary mind and usurp his holy position.
If I do not present this verse on the mind, I shall ultimately not obtain the Dharma."
After reflecting for a long time, [he thought,] "This is most difficult, most difficult!

When the night reached the third watch, he ensured no one saw him and then inscribed a verse of presenting his mind upon the central wall of the southern corridor, desiring to seek the dharma of the robe.
"If the Fifth Patriarch sees this verse and says its words are worthy, and if he comes to seek me out, I shall tell the Master that it was Xiu who composed it.

If the Fifth Patriarch sees the verse and says it is inadequate, I will consider it my own delusion; that my karmic obstructions from past lives are too heavy to have been worthy of receiving the Dharma; and that the Sage’s intention is unfathomable, so I shall let my mind rest."
At the third watch, Elder Xiu took a candle and inscribed a verse upon the central wall of the southern corridor; no one knew of it.
The verse reads:
“The body is the Bodhi tree, The mind is a stand for a bright mirror.”
"From time to time, diligently sweep and wipe it, / And do not let dust and grime settle upon it.
After the Elder Shenxiu had finished composing this verse for the seventh time, he returned to his room and lay down; no one saw him.
At dawn the following day, the Fifth Patriarch summoned Lu Gongfeng to the south corridor to paint the *Laṅkāvatāra* transformation scene.
Suddenly, the Fifth Patriarch saw this verse; having finished reading it, he said to the artist:
"Hongren gives you thirty thousand coins, Gongfeng, for your great trouble in traveling from afar; there is no need to paint the transformation scene."
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"All that has form is merely illusory.
It would be better to preserve this verse and have those who are deluded recite it.
"By practicing in accordance with this, one does not fall into the three evil realms;
by practicing in accordance with the Dharma, people will receive great benefit.
Thereupon, the Great Master summoned all his disciples to come, burned incense before the verse, and once everyone had entered and seen him, they all conceived a heart of reverence.
Hongren said, "Only those of you who can recite this verse in its entirety shall realize their nature; by practicing according to it, you will not fall.
The disciples all recited it and were filled with reverence, exclaiming, "Excellent!"
The Fifth Patriarch then summoned the Venerable Xiu into the hall and asked,
"Was it you who composed this verse?
If it was you, you should receive my Dharma."
The Elder Xiu said:
"It is my fault!
It was indeed composed by Shenxiu."

"I do not dare to seek the Patriarch’s favor, but I pray that the Venerable Master will, out of compassion, examine whether this disciple possesses a modicum of wisdom or understands the Great Meaning.
The Fifth Patriarch said, "In composing this verse, your understanding has only reached the gate; you have not yet been able to enter."
If ordinary beings practice according to this verse, they will not fall;
yet, if they form such a view while seeking unsurpassed enlightenment, it cannot be attained.
"You must be able to enter the gate and see your own original nature.

Go for now; reflect upon this for a day or two, and then compose another verse to present to me. If you can enter the gate and see your own original nature, I shall entrust to you the robe and the Dharma."
Several days after the Senior Monk Xiu had departed, [Xuedou] was unable to compose it.
In the eighth section, there was a young boy passing by the mill who was chanting this verse.
Upon hearing this once, Huineng realized he had not yet seen his own nature,
yet he immediately grasped the general meaning. He asked the boy, "What verse did you just recite?"

The youth replied, "You do not know that the Great Master spoke of the great importance of the matter of birth and death. He wished to transmit the robe and the Dharma, instructing his disciples each to compose a verse to present to him; whoever realizes the Great Meaning shall be granted the robe and the Dharma and acknowledged as the Sixth Patriarch."

There was an elder named Shenxiu who suddenly inscribed a verse on the absence of marks beneath the southern corridor. The Fifth Patriarch ordered all his disciples to recite it, saying that whoever realized this verse would see their own nature;
by practicing according to it, one would attain liberation.

Huìnéng replied, "I have been treading the pestle for over eight months now, yet I have not reached the hall. I hope you, Venerable Sir, will lead me to the southern corridor so that I may see this verse and pay my respects; I also wish to recite it to establish a karmic connection for future lives and aspire to be born in the Buddha-ground."
The youth led Huineng down to the southern corridor, where Huineng immediately prostrated himself and recited this verse.
Because he was illiterate, he requested someone to read it aloud;
upon hearing it, Huineng immediately grasped its general meaning.

Huīnéng also composed a verse and, having secured a scribe, had it inscribed upon the western wall to present his own fundamental mind: "If one does not recognize the fundamental mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit; by recognizing the mind and seeing its nature, one immediately awakens to the Great Meaning."
Huineng’s verse says:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror likewise has no stand.
The Buddha-nature is eternally pure; Where could there be any dust?"
Furthermore, a verse says:
"The mind is the Bodhi tree, The body is the stand for the bright mirror.
Since the bright mirror is fundamentally pure, Where could dust and grime stain it?"
When the disciples within the monastery saw that Huineng could compose such a verse, they were all astonished; Huineng, however, returned to the rice-hulling shed.
Suddenly, the Fifth Patriarch came down the corridor and, seeing Huineng’s verse, immediately recognized its profound meaning.
Fearing that the multitude might find out, the Fifth Patriarch said to them,
"This matter is not yet finished.
On the ninth day, at the third watch of the night, the Fifth Patriarch summoned Huineng to his quarters and expounded the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon hearing this once, Huineng attained enlightenment instantly.
That night he received the Dharma, unknown to anyone, and was immediately entrusted with the teaching of Sudden Enlightenment and the robe, becoming the Sixth Patriarch.
The robe shall be used as a token of transmission, handed down from generation to generation;
the Dharma is transmitted mind-to-mind, and you must cause it to be realized within yourself.
Thus spoke the Fifth Patriarch.
"Huineng! Since ancient times, the transmission of the Dharma has been as precarious as a thread hanging from the air!
If you remain here, someone may harm you; you must depart at once."
Regarding the tenth section, the method for Huineng obtaining the robe: He set out at the third watch.
The Fifth Patriarch personally escorted him as far as Jiuyang Station, where they parted immediately. The Fifth Patriarch instructed him: "Go now and exert yourself in carrying the Dharma southward.

Do not propagate this Dharma for three years; it will be difficult to leave here, but you shall later spread the teachings and skillfully guide those who are deluded. If they attain the opening of their minds, they will be no different from my own realization."
Having finished his parting words, he set out toward the south.

During the eleventh month, while traveling through the two-month interval, he reached Dayu Ridge. Unbeknownst to him, several hundred men had followed behind with the intent to seize Huineng and take back his robes and Dharma; however, when they reached the midpoint of the road, they all turned back.

There was only one monk, surnamed Chen and named Huishun; he had previously been a third-grade general and was coarse and wicked by nature. He went straight up the ridge and came to pursue and seize him.
Huineng immediately returned the Dharma robe and again refused to accept it.
Huishun said, "I have come from afar specifically to seek the Dharma; I do not desire the robe."
On the mountain peak, he was able to transmit the Dharma to Huishun; upon hearing it, Huishun’s mind opened instantly, and he was able to immediately turn northward to transform others.
In the twelfth chapter, Huineng comes to this place; he shares with the officials, clergy, and laity the causes and conditions accumulated over many kalpas.
This teaching was transmitted by the former sages; it is not something Huineng knows of himself.

Those who wish to hear the teachings of the former sages must each purify their minds; having heard and understood them, they should vow to eliminate their own delusions, as the sages of past generations awakened to this Dharma below.
Master Huineng called out, "Virtuous friends!"

The wisdom of Bodhi and Prajna is inherently possessed by all people of the world; it is only because their minds are deluded that they cannot awaken to it themselves, and thus must seek out a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to show them the Way and enable them to see their own nature.
"Good friend!

Whether one is a fool or a wise person, their Buddha-nature is fundamentally without distinction; it is solely due to delusion and awakening. When deluded, one is a fool; when awakened, one becomes wise."
The Thirteenth Chapter: "Good friend!
This Dharma-gate of mine takes concentration and wisdom as its foundation.
First, do not be deluded by thinking that wisdom and concentration are distinct; the essence of concentration and wisdom is one and non-dual."
Concentration is the very substance of wisdom, and wisdom is the function of concentration.
At the very moment of wisdom, concentration resides within wisdom; at the very moment of concentration, wisdom resides within concentration.
O Good Friends!
This principle refers precisely to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

When a practitioner on the path of training applies their attention, they should not say that concentration arises first and gives rise to wisdom, or that wisdom arises first and gives rise to concentration, as if concentration and wisdom were separate and distinct.
One who holds such a view perceives phenomena as having two distinct characteristics: the mouth speaks what is good while the mind is not good, and thus concentration and wisdom are unequal;
when both mind and mouth are good, the internal and external are of one kind, and concentration and wisdom are equal.
Cultivation through self-awakening does not lie in verbal contention.
To argue over priority is to be a deluded person.
If one does not cease the pursuit of victory and defeat, one will instead give rise to the notions of "Dharma" and "self," remaining inseparable from the four marks.
The fourteenth section: "As for the *ekavyūha-samādhi*, it consists of always practicing a straightforward mind at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down."
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment; a straightforward mind is the pure land.

Do not let your mind and actions be crooked while your mouth preaches straightforwardness, nor preach the Samādhi of One Practice with your mouth while failing to practice a straightforward mind; such a person is not a disciple of the Buddha.
Simply practicing with a straightforward mind, having no attachment toward any phenomena, is called the Samādhi of Single Practice.

Deluded people become attached to the marks of phenomena and cling to the Samādhi of Single Practice, claiming that merely sitting motionless, eliminating delusions, and not giving rise to thoughts constitutes the Samādhi of Single Practice.
If it were thus, this dharma would be identical to insentient matter and would instead become a cause and condition for obstructing the Way.
The Way must flow freely; why then does it become stagnant?
When the mind does not dwell upon dharmas, the Way flows freely; when it dwells, it becomes bound.
If sitting motionless were correct, then Vimalakīrti would not have rebuked Śāriputra for his practice of seated meditation in the forest.
Good friend!
Furthermore, I see people who instruct others to sit, to observe the mind, to observe purity, and to remain unmoving and unarisen, thereby applying their efforts from this point forward.

Deluded people do not awaken, but instead cling to these [teachings] and fall into error; there are thus hundreds of such ways of instructing and guiding, and therefore one should know that they are all greatly mistaken.
The fifteenth refutation: "O Good Knowledge!..."
What are concentration and wisdom like?
They are like a lamp and its light: where there is a lamp, there is light; where there is no lamp, there is no light.
The lamp is the substance of the light, and the light is the function of the lamp.
The names are two, yet their substance is not of two kinds.
This Dharma of concentration and wisdom is likewise so.
Chapter Sixteen: "O Good Spiritual Friend!..."
The Dharma has neither sudden nor gradual aspects; it is the people who possess sharp or dull faculties.
For those who are deluded, one provides gradual exhortation; for those who have awakened, one practices suddenly.
To recognize one's own fundamental mind is to see one's original nature; once awakened, there is originally no distinction, yet without awakening, one wanders in saṃsāra through long kalpas.
Act XVII: "O Good Friend!
This Dharma-gate of mine, from its inception until now, whether sudden or gradual, establishes non-thought as its school, formlessness as its essence, and non-abiding as its root."
What is called "signlessness"?
Signlessness means being free from signs amidst signs.
What is called "mindfulnesslessness" (non-thought)? Mindfulnesslessness means not thinking amidst thought.

Non-abiding is the inherent nature of human beings; from moment to moment there is no abiding. The preceding thought, the present thought, and the succeeding thought continue one after another in an uninterrupted succession.
If for even a single thought-moment there is a severance, the Dharma-body immediately departs from the form-body.
Within every moment of thought, one should abide nowhere among all phenomena.
If for a single thought-moment one abides, then every successive thought-moment will abide; this is called bondage.
Regarding all phenomena, not dwelling for even a single thought-moment is itself freedom from bondage; therefore, non-dwelling is the foundation.
Good friend!
To be externally detached from all marks is formlessness.
Simply by being able to remain detached from signs, the essential nature is pure.
Therefore, taking signlessness as its essence and remaining unstained amidst all objects is called "non-thought" (amanasikāra).
Regarding one's own mindfulness, remain detached from external objects and do not give rise to thoughts concerning phenomena.
Do not leave all things unthought; if you exhaustively eliminate all thoughts, the single thought will be severed and vanish, and you will be reborn in another place.
Among those who study the Way, there are none who do not understand the meaning of the Dharma.
Yet, while their own errors are still forgivable, they go further by encouraging others into delusion; failing to recognize their own confusion, they even slander the scriptures and the Dharma.
For this reason, I establish non-thought as the fundamental principle.
This is because when deluded people give rise to thought regarding objects, false views immediately arise upon that thought, and all defilements and delusive thoughts are born from this.

However, this teaching establishes non-thought as its fundamental principle; yet worldly people distance themselves from seeing and fail to give rise to thought. If there were no thought at all, even "non-thought" could not be established.
What is there that is "non-existent"?
What is it that is "recalled"?
"Non-existence" refers to being free from the two marks and all afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Mindfulness" refers to mindfulness of the original nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
True Suchness is the substance of mindfulness, while mindfulness is the function of True Suchness.
When the self-nature gives rise to mindfulness, although it involves seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, it remains unstained by the myriad objects of experience and is ever-sovereign.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Externally, one is able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena; internally, one remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Chapter Eighteen: "O Good Friend!..."
In this Dharma-gate, the practice of seated meditation does not originally involve attachment to the mind, nor attachment to purity, nor even the state of immovability.
If one speaks of "observing the mind," the mind is originally illusory; because illusion is like a phantom, there is nothing to observe.
If you say that one observes purity, the human nature is fundamentally pure; it is because of deluded thoughts that True Suchness (Tathatā) is covered over.
When one leaves behind deluded thoughts, the original nature is pure.
If you do not perceive that the self-nature is fundamentally pure, yet give rise to a mind to observe purity, you will instead produce the delusion of purity; such delusions have no fixed location.
Therefore, know that the act of "observing" is itself delusion.
Purity is formless, yet one establishes a mark of purity and claims it is a spiritual practice; those who harbor such a view obstruct their own original nature and become bound by purity.
If one cultivates immovability, not seeing the faults or afflictions of any person is itself the immovability of self-nature.
When a deluded person remains physically unmoving yet opens their mouth to speak of others' right and wrong, they contradict the Way.
To watch the mind and watch for purity is, in fact, a cause and condition that obstructs the Way.
Chapter Nineteen: "Now that it is thus, within this Dharma-gate, what is called 'sitting in meditation'?"

Within this Dharma-gate, all things are unimpeded; to not give rise to discursive thoughts regarding any external objects is "sitting," and to see the fundamental nature without distraction is "meditation."
What is meant by dhyāna-samādhi?
To be free from external signs is called dhyāna; to be undisturbed within is called samādhi.
When one is free from external signs, the internal nature remains undisturbed.

The inherent nature being naturally pure is called concentration (*samādhi*); it is only because of contact with objects that there is distraction. When one is free from such characteristics and is not distracted, that is concentration.

Being free from characteristics externally is *dhyāna*, and being undisturbed internally is *samādhi*; thus, external *dhyāna* and internal *samādhi* together are termed "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"At that moment, there was a sudden breakthrough, and he recovered his original mind.
The *Brahmajāla Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra* states:
"The original source and fundamental nature are pure. Good friend!

Seeing that one's own nature is inherently pure, one cultivates and acts for oneself as the Dharma-body of one's own nature; one practices the conduct of the Buddha and brings about the realization of the Buddha-way for oneself.
Act Twenty: "Good friends!
You must all personally receive the formless precepts.
At this moment, following what Huineng speaks, let the good friends perceive the Buddha of the Three Bodies within yourselves."
In one's own physical body, take refuge in the Pure Dharma-body Buddha;
in one's own physical body, take refuge in the thousand, hundred, and ten billion Transformation-body Buddhas;
in one's own physical body, take refuge in the future Perfect Reward-body Buddha.

The above three invocations state that the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is one's dwelling and cannot be said to be "returned to. The aforementioned three bodies reside within one's own *dharmatā*; all worldly people possess them, yet they fail to see them due to delusion. They seek the Tathāgata of the three bodies externally, failing to perceive the Buddha of the three bodies within their own form-body.
"O virtuous friend!

Listen as I speak to you, virtuous friend, so that you may perceive within your own physical body the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the three bodies of the Buddha; these three bodies of the Buddha arise from your own intrinsic nature."
What is meant by the Buddha of the Pure Dharma-body?
Good friend!
The nature of worldly people is inherently pure; the myriad dharmas reside within their own nature.
When one contemplates all evil matters, one immediately engages in evil conduct;
when one contemplates all wholesome matters, one then cultivates wholesome conduct.
One should know that all such phenomena are entirely contained within self-nature (*svabhāva*); this self-nature is eternally pure, and the sun and moon are eternally luminous.

It is simply because clouds cover it that what is above is bright while what is below is dark, preventing one from clearly seeing the sun, moon, and stars; yet when suddenly encountering a favorable breeze that blows away and completely rolls up the clouds and mist, the myriad phenomena of the universe all appear at once.
The nature of sentient beings is pure, like the clear sky.
Their wisdom is like the sun, and their insight is like the moon; thus, wisdom and insight are ever-luminous.
Yet, when they become attached to external objects, the floating clouds of deluded thoughts cover them, so that their inherent nature cannot shine forth.

Encountering a virtuous friend, one is opened to the true and correct Dharma; delusion and confusion are blown away, and both within and without become clear and transparent. Within one's own nature, all phenomena manifest.
All phenomena abide in their own nature;
this is called the pure Dharma-body.
To take refuge in oneself means to eliminate unwholesome thoughts and unwholesome actions; this is what is meant by taking refuge.
What is meant by the "thousand billion transformation Buddhas"?
When there is no deliberation, the nature is empty and quiescent;
when there is deliberation, it is the self-manifestation [of the Buddha].
Contemplating unwholesome dharmas transforms one into a hell-being;
contemplating wholesome dharmas transforms one into a heavenly being;
contemplating poison and harm transforms one into an animal.
Contemplating compassion, one transforms into a bodhisattva;
contemplating wisdom, one transforms into the upper realms;
contemplating ignorance, one transforms into the lower regions.
The manifestations of the self-nature are exceedingly numerous, yet deluded people do not know or perceive them themselves.
When a single thought of goodness arises, wisdom is immediately produced; this is called the Self-Nature Transformation Body Buddha (Nirmāṇakāya).
What is meant by the Perfect Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*)?
A single lamp can dispel the darkness of a thousand years; a single moment of wisdom can extinguish the folly of ten thousand years.
Do not dwell on the past, but always contemplate what lies ahead; constantly maintaining virtuous thoughts for the future is called the Reward Body.
A single thought of evil repays a thousand years of a virtuous mind;
a single thought of goodness extinguishes a thousand years of evil.
Since the advent of impermanence, a subsequent thought of goodness is called the "recompense body" (pāribhogika-kāya).
To contemplate from the perspective of the Dharmakāya is itself the Nirmāṇakāya;
every thought-moment of goodness is the Saṃbhogakāya.
To awaken and cultivate for oneself is what is called taking refuge.
Skin and flesh constitute the physical body, and the physical body is but a dwelling; it is not that which one takes refuge in.
Rather, by awakening to the three bodies (trikāya), one recognizes the Great Meaning.
In the twenty-first chapter: "Now that you have personally taken refuge in the Buddha of the Three Bodies, together with your spiritual friends, you shall give rise to the Four Great Vows."
"Good friend!
At one time, I followed Huineng’s path and made these three vows:

'Sentient beings are boundless, I vow to deliver them; afflictions are boundless, I vow to sever them; Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to study them; the unsurpassed Buddha-way, I vow to accomplish.'"
"Good friends!

'The boundless multitude of sentient beings I vow to deliver' does not mean that I, Huineng, shall deliver them; rather, the sentient beings within the minds of you, good friends, must each deliver themselves by means of their own body and their own inherent nature."
What is meant by "delivering oneself through one's own nature"?

Within one's own physical form, there exist false views, afflictions, ignorance, and delusion; yet within these, there is inherently the nature of original enlightenment, which delivers [the self] by means of right view.
Having realized the wisdom of right view and prajñā, one eliminates ignorance, delusion, and false views.

Each and every sentient being crosses over by themselves: when the heterodox comes, they cross over with the orthodox; when delusion comes, they cross over with awakening; when folly comes, they cross over with wisdom; when evil comes, they cross over with goodness; when afflictions come, they cross over with bodhi. To cross over in this manner is called true crossing-over.
I vow to sever all boundless afflictions, eliminating delusions from my own mind.
I vow to study all boundless Dharma gates, learning the unsurpassed True Dharma.

I vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way; constantly practicing with a humble mind, revering all beings, and remaining far removed from deluded attachments, may awakening wisdom give birth to prajñā. Having cast off confusion and folly, I shall personally realize the accomplishment of the Buddha-way through the power of my vows.

The twenty-second chapter: "Now that the Four Great Vows have been made, one receives from the spiritual friend the formless repentance to extinguish the karmic obstacles of the three periods of time."
The Great Master said:
"O Good Knowledge!
Whether it be the preceding thought, the succeeding thought, or the present thought—moment after moment, they are not defiled by folly or delusion."
All past evil deeds are removed at once; if their inherent nature is removed, that is repentance.

If every preceding thought, succeeding thought, and the present thought are not stained by ignorance from moment to moment, and if the former mind of deceit is cast off, its permanent severance is called repentance of the self-nature.

The preceding thought, the subsequent thought, and the present thought—moment by moment, may they not be stained by illness. Having eliminated all prior jealousy, if the self-nature is thus cleared away, this constitutes repentance. (Chanted three times.)
"Good friend!
What is meant by 'repentance' (chanhui)?
'Chan' means not to commit [the offense] again for the rest of one's life; 'hui' means recognizing one's previous errors."

Evil karma never departs from the mind; speaking with one's mouth before the Buddhas is of no benefit. Within this Dharma gate of mine, to forever sever [evil] and refrain from committing it is called repentance.
In the twenty-third chapter: "Now that the confession has been completed, the Preceptor bestows upon the spiritual friend the precepts of the Three Refuges of Non-characteristic.
The Master said:
"Spiritual friend!..."
I take refuge in the Awakened One, the Most Honored among Two-legged Beings;
I take refuge in the Righteous One, the Most Honored among those Free from Desire;
I take refuge in the Pure One, the Most Honored among the Multitude.
From this day forward, I shall call the Buddha my Teacher and shall no longer take refuge in other heterodox or deluded outsiders; may the compassion of the Triple Gem bear witness to this.
O Good Friends!
Huineng exhorts you, O good friends, to take refuge in the Triple Gem:
"Buddha" means awakening;
"Dharma" means correctness.
"Seng" (Saṃgha) means purity.
When one's own mind takes refuge in awakening, delusion and error do not arise; with few desires and contentment, one is detached from wealth and form—this is called the Honored One of Two Feet.

Because one’s own mind takes refuge in the correct and remains free from error in every thought-moment, there is no attachment; being free from attachment, one is called the Honored One Who is Free from Desire.

Because one’s own mind takes refuge in the pure, although all defilements and deluded thoughts exist within the self-nature, the self-nature is not stained by them; thus, one is called the Honored One Among the Multitudes.
Ordinary people do not understand this; day after day they receive the precepts of the Three Refuges.
If one says, "I take refuge in the Buddha," where is the Buddha?
If one does not see the Buddha, there is nothing to which one can take refuge.
Since there is nowhere to which one can return, such words are actually false.
Good friends!
Each of you should observe for yourselves; do not misapply your minds. The sutras state only that one takes refuge in the Buddha oneself; they do not say one takes refuge in another Buddha.
The self-nature does not return [to anything], as it has no place of reliance.
Chapter Twenty-four: "Now that you have taken refuge in the Triple Gem, each of you should with a sincere heart speak the Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā to your spiritual friends."
Although the good friends could not understand what was being contemplated, Huineng explained it to them, and they each listened.
"Mahāprajñāpāramitā" is a term from the Sanskrit language of the Western regions; in the language of Tang, it means "Great Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore."
This Dharma must be practiced; it does not reside in verbal recitation.
If one recites with the mouth but does not practice, it is like an illusion or a transformation.
For the practitioner, the Dharma-body is equal to that of the Buddha.
What is meant by "Mahā"? Mahā means great.
The measure of the mind is vast and expansive, like empty space.
If one sits in meditation with an empty mind, one falls into the emptiness of the indeterminate.

Just as space can contain the sun, moon, and stars; the great earth, mountains, and rivers; all grasses and trees; the wicked and the virtuous; evil dharmas and wholesome dharmas; and even heaven and hell—all exist within space, so too is the emptiness of human nature.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter: "Nature Encompasses Myriad Dharmas is Great. All myriad dharmas are entirely one's own nature.

Seeing all people and non-people, the evil and the good, as well as unwholesome and wholesome dharmas, one does not abandon any of them, yet remains unstained by them, just like empty space; this is called "Great," and this is the practice of Mahā.
The deluded recite with their mouths; the wise practice with their minds.
Furthermore, there are those who are deluded who claim that being empty-minded and free from thought constitutes greatness; this, too, is not correct.
The scope of the mind is vast; do not practice what is petty.
Do not merely speak empty words; if you do not cultivate this practice, you are not my disciple.
Chapter Twenty-Six: "What is called Prajñā?"
Prajñā is wisdom.
At all times, to be free from delusion in every thought-moment and to constantly practice wisdom is what is called the practice of Prajñā.
A single moment of delusion severs Prajñā; a single moment of wisdom gives rise to Prajñā.
The minds of worldly people are constantly deluded, yet they say of themselves, "I am practicing Prajñā.
Prajñā has no form or characteristics; its very nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
What, then, is called a *pāramitā*?
This is the Sanskrit term from the Western land; in the language of Tang, it means "reaching the other shore.
To understand its meaning is to transcend arising and ceasing; when one clings to objects, arising and ceasing arise.
It is like water having waves: this is precisely being on this shore.
Detached from objects, there is neither arising nor ceasing; like water flowing eternally, it is therefore called "reaching the other shore," and thus named *pāramitā*.
The deluded recite it with their mouths, while the wise practice it with their minds.
When mindfulness arises, there is delusion; where there is delusion, it is not true reality.
If one acts with every thought-moment, this is called true reality.
One who awakens to this Dharma awakens to the Dharma of Prajñā and cultivates the practice of Prajñā.
If one does not practice, one remains an ordinary person; if one practices for even a single thought-moment, one’s Dharma-body is equal to that of a Buddha.
Good friend!
Afflictions themselves are bodhi.
If the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary person; if the succeeding thought is awakened, one is a Buddha.
Good friends!
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā is most honored, most supreme, and foremost; it is without abiding, without going, and without coming.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge from within this; by means of great wisdom, they reach the other shore, shattering the five aggregates, afflictions, and worldly toil—most honored, most supreme, and foremost.
Praising the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle, one practices and will surely attain Buddhahood.

Without going, without staying, and without coming or departing, this is the equality of concentration and wisdom. It is unstained by any phenomena; from within it, the Buddhas of the three periods of time transform the three poisons into precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: "O Good Friend!
This Dharma-gate of mine gives rise to eighty-four thousand wisdoms from a single prajñā. Why is this?"
Sentient beings in the world have eighty-four thousand afflictions; if there were no afflictions, Prajñā would be ever-present, never departing from its own nature.
One who awakens to this Dharma is one of non-thought, non-recollection, and non-attachment.
Do not give rise to deception or falsehood; this is itself the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).
By employing wisdom to contemplate and illuminate, neither grasping at nor rejecting any phenomena, one immediately perceives the nature and attains the Buddha-way.
The Twenty-eighth Chapter: "Good friend!

If you wish to enter the profound Dharma-realm and attain the samādhi of Prajñā, you must directly cultivate the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā. By merely holding this single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, you will immediately realize your nature and enter the samādhi of Prajñā."
One should know that the merit of such a person is immeasurable; though it is clearly praised in the sūtras, it cannot be fully described.
This is the vehicle of the supreme dharma, taught for those of great wisdom and superior faculties.
If those of inferior faculties hear the Dharma, faith does not arise in their minds.

Why is this? It is like a great dragon that, when sending down heavy rain upon Jambudvīpa, causes cities, towns, and villages to all drift away, just as if they were blades of grass being carried off by the current.
If a great rain falls, falling upon the great ocean, it neither increases nor decreases.
So too, when those of the Great Vehicle hear the teaching of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, their minds open and they attain awakening and understanding.
Therefore, know that the original nature inherently possesses the wisdom of *prajñā*; one employs this wisdom for contemplative observation without relying on words and letters.

It is like rainwater, which does not originate from the heavens, but is originally drawn forth by the Dragon King from the rivers and seas, causing all sentient beings, all plants and trees, and all things animate and inanimate to receive its nourishment.
Just as all streams and currents flow back into the great ocean, and the ocean receives these many waters, merging them into a single entity,
so too is the nature of sentient beings— the wisdom of prajñā.

The twenty-ninth chapter: "As for those of inferior capacity, when they hear this teaching of sudden enlightenment, it is like the grasses and trees upon the great earth whose root-natures are inherently small; if they are drenched by a great rain, they all simply topple over and cannot grow."
Those of inferior faculties are likewise so.
Possessing the wisdom of *prajñā*, they are no different from those of great wisdom.
For what reason do they not awaken upon hearing the Dharma?
Because the obstacles of wrong views are heavy and the roots of affliction are deep, it is like a great cloud covering the sun; if it is not blown away by the wind, the sun cannot manifest.

The wisdom of Prajñā likewise has neither small nor great; yet because all sentient beings possess deluded minds and seek the Buddha through external cultivation without awakening to their own nature, they are people of small capacity.

Having heard this sudden teaching, they no longer believed in external cultivation; rather, within their own minds, they caused their own fundamental nature to constantly give rise to right view. At that moment, all false views, afflictions, and the weary masses were fully awakened, just as the great ocean receives all streams—small waters and large waters merging into a single essence—which is precisely what it means to see one's nature.

Neither abiding within nor without, coming and going with freedom, one is able to eliminate the grasping mind and attain unimpeded penetration; if the mind cultivates this practice, it is essentially no different from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The Thirtieth Chapter: "All scriptures and written words—the Small and Great Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon—are all established based on persons; they are thus able to be instituted because of the nature of wisdom."
If there were no people in this world, then all phenomena would fundamentally not exist either.
Therefore, we know that all phenomena originally arise from people, and all scriptures exist because they are spoken by people.
The conditions for this lie in the fact that among human beings there are both the ignorant and the wise; the ignorant are small persons, while the wise are great persons.
When a deluded person questions a wise one, the wise person expounds the Dharma for the sake of the ignorant, causing the ignorant one to awaken, understand, and have their mind opened.
If those who are deluded awaken and their minds open, they are no different from those of great wisdom.
Thus we know that if one does not awaken, even a Buddha is but a sentient being;
yet if one awakens in a single thought-moment, even a sentient being is a Buddha.
Therefore, know that all phenomena are entirely contained within one's own mind; why not suddenly perceive the true nature of *tathatā* from within this very mind?
The *Brahmajāla Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra* states:
"The fundamental source and original nature are pure."
"When consciousness awakens to the mind and one perceives the nature, one spontaneously accomplishes the Buddha-way.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:
"At that moment, there is sudden clarity, and one regains the original mind."
"Chapter Thirty-One: 'Good friend!
Under the guidance of my Preceptor Ren, upon hearing his words but once, I attained great enlightenment and suddenly beheld my true nature, the Suchness of reality.'"

Therefore, so that the teachings of sudden enlightenment may circulate in future generations, I cause those who study the Way to suddenly awaken to Bodhi; each shall contemplate their own mind, causing their own fundamental nature to suddenly awaken.
If you cannot awaken on your own, you must seek out a great spiritual friend (*mahā-kalyāṇamitra*) to show you the Way and enable you to see your nature.
What is meant by a "great spiritual friend"?
One who understands the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttara-yāna*) and directly points out the correct path is a great spiritual friend; this is a great cause and condition.
The reason for manifesting the Way is to enable one to realize their true nature.
All wholesome dharmas are initiated through the great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
The twelve divisions of the scriptures of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are inherently possessed within the human nature.
If one cannot awaken to the self-nature by oneself, one must rely on a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to point out the Way and enable the seeing of one's nature.
If one awakens by oneself, there is no need to seek a spiritual friend externally.
If one seeks liberation by seeking a spiritual friend externally, such a thing is impossible.
If one recognizes the true spiritual friend within one's own mind, one immediately attains liberation.
However, if one's own mind is deluded and inverted by false thoughts, even if external spiritual friends provide instruction, salvation cannot be achieved.

If you do not attain self-awakening, you should give rise to the contemplation of *prajñā*; in a single instant, all deluded thoughts will be extinguished, which is itself the true and genuine spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and upon this one awakening, you shall immediately reach the stage of Buddhahood.
The ground of the mind is its own nature; by observing it with wisdom, both within and without become clear and transparent, and one recognizes one's own original mind.
If one recognizes the original mind, that is itself liberation.
Having attained liberation is precisely the samādhi of prajñā.
To awaken to the samādhi of prajñā is non-thought (amanasikāra).
What is meant by non-thought?
As for the Dharma of non-thought: one perceives all dharmas yet does not cling to any dharma;
one pervades all places yet does not cling to any place.

With the self-nature eternally pure, one causes the six thieves to flee from the six gates; amidst the six sense-objects, one neither departs nor is stained, coming and going with freedom. This is precisely the *prajñā-samādhi*, the liberation of mastery, and is called the practice of non-thought.
Do not think of any phenomena; you must cause all thoughts to cease. To do so is to be bound by the Dharma, which is termed an extreme view.
One who awakens to the Dharma of non-thought penetrates all phenomena;
one who awakens to the Dharma of non-thought perceives the realm of all Buddhas.
Those who awaken to the sudden dharma of non-thought reach the stage of Buddhahood.
The thirty-second chapter states: "O Good Knowledge!
Those in future generations who attain my Dharma will constantly see my Dharma-body not departing from your side."
"Good friends!

If you take this sudden teaching of the Dharma, seeing it together and practicing it together, making vows to receive and uphold it, and thus maintaining such Buddhist teachings throughout your lives without falling back, and if you wish to enter the ranks of the sages, you must receive its transmission. Since time immemorial, the robe and the Dharma have been transmitted in silence; if you make a great vow not to retreat from Bodhi, then you must be entrusted with them."

If one’s views do not accord with this and one lacks the necessary resolve, one must not propagate it recklessly in any place whatsoever; to do so would harm those who came before and ultimately yield no benefit.
"If foolish people do not understand and slander this Dharma-gate, they will sever the Buddha-nature for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
The Thirty-third Patriarch said:
"O Good Friend!
"Listen to my recitation of the 'Verse on Formlessness' (Animitta-gāthā), which shall extinguish the sins of you who are deluded; it is also called the 'Verse on the Extinction of Sin'.
The verse says:
"The fool cultivates merit but does not cultivate the Path, Claiming that the cultivation of merit is itself the Path."
The merit of giving and making offerings is boundless, yet the three karmas within the mind remain as they were.
If one seeks to extinguish transgressions by cultivating merit, though one gains blessings in future lives, the original transgressions persist.
If one understands that the mind of directionality eliminates the conditions for transgression, one performs true repentance within the nature of each thing.
If one awakens to the true repentance of the Mahāyāna, eliminating deviant conduct and abiding in the correct, there is no transgression.
If those who study the Way can observe themselves, they are of the same category as those who have attained awakening.
I, Huineng, now transmit this teaching of sudden enlightenment; may those who study it realize their identity with the One Body.
If you wish to seek the Dharma-body in the future, Wash the evil conditions of the three poisons within your mind.
Exert yourself in the Way; do not be idle, Lest you suddenly waste this entire life in vain.
"If one encounters the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, one should reverently join one's palms and seek it with a sincere heart.

When the Great Master had finished preaching the Dharma, Wei the Prefect, the officials, the monastic community, and the laypeople—both clergy and laity—praised it endlessly, saying it was something they had never heard before.
In the thirty-fourth chapter, the Prefect prostrated himself and said:
"The Master’s preaching of the Dharma is truly inconceivable.
I still have a slight doubt, which I wish to ask of the Master."
"I hope that Master Wanyi, in your great kindness and great compassion, will explain this for your disciple.
The Great Master said, "If you have a doubt, ask it immediately; why must you do so repeatedly?"
The Prefect asked:
"Is this the Dharma?
Is it the essential teaching of the Patriarch Bodhidharma, the foremost master of the Western Land?"
The Great Master said,
“It is so! The Prefect asked:
"The disciple saw it said that Master Bodhidharma was transforming Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
The Emperor asked Bodhidharma:
'Throughout my life, have I gained any merit from building monasteries, practicing charity, and making offerings?'"
Bodhidharma replied,
"There are none. Emperor Wu was filled with regret and subsequently ordered Bodhidharma to leave the country.
"I do not yet understand these words; I beg the Master to explain them.
The Sixth Patriarch said, "In truth, there is no merit. Your Excellency, do not doubt the words of Master Bodhidharma."
"Emperor Wu adhered to heterodox paths and did not recognize the True Dharma.
The Prefect asked: "Why was there no merit?"
The Upādhyāya said:
"Building monasteries, practicing giving, and making offerings merely cultivate merit (puṇya).
One must not mistake merit for spiritual accomplishment (guṇa). Spiritual accomplishment resides in the Dharma-body; it does not reside in the field of merit."

The qualities exist inherently within the nature of phenomena; being impartial and upright is the Buddha-nature. If one outwardly practices respect but inwardly treats all people with contempt and does not sever the sense of "I," then one possesses no qualities at all.
Intrinsic nature has no merit, and the Dharma-body has no merit.
To practice the mind of equality and straightforwardness in every thought-moment is itself non-contemptuous virtue.
Constantly practicing respect is the "function" (功) of cultivating one's own body, while cultivating one's own mind is the "virtue" (德).
"Merit is created by one's own mind; 'blessing' (fu) and 'merit' (gongde) are distinct.
Emperor Wu did not understand the correct principle; it was not the fault of the Great Master.
The Third-Fifth [Patriarch] bowed to the Prefect and asked again:
"The disciple observes that both monastics and laypeople constantly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, aspiring to be reborn in the Western Land.
I request that you, Venerable Master, explain whether or not they can attain birth there;
I hope you will dispel my doubts."
The Great Master said:
"May your lordship listen as I explain it to you.

When the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī, he spoke of the Western Land to guide and transform beings; the scriptural text is clear that it is not far from here, yet this was taught specifically for those of inferior capacity."
Speaking of the near and speaking of the far is solely due to superior intelligence.
People themselves are of two kinds, but the Dharma has no dual nature.
There are differences between delusion and awakening; there are variations in the speed of insight.
Those who are deluded seek rebirth in that land through the recitation of the Buddha's name, whereas those who have attained awakening purify their own minds.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure."
"Your Excellency!
In the East, one is without fault provided the mind is pure; in the West, there is transgression if the mind is impure.
For those who are deluded, they wish to be reborn in the East or the West; for those who have awakened, wherever they may be, it is all of one kind."
If the mind is simply free from impurity, the Western Land is not far from here;
if the mind gives rise to impure thoughts, it will be difficult to reach rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha.
To eliminate the ten evils is equivalent to traveling one hundred thousand miles.
If one is free from the eight heterodoxies, one transcends them by eight thousand;
yet by practicing only with a straightforward mind, one arrives as quickly as a finger-snap. My Lord!
If you simply practice the ten wholesome deeds, why must you further aspire for rebirth there?
If you do not sever the mind of the ten unwholesome deeds, which Buddha will come to welcome and invite you?
If you awaken to the sudden teaching of non-arising, you will see that the Western Land is but a mere instant away.
"If one does not awaken to the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, the path to rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha is far; how then can one reach it?
The Sixth Patriarch said, "I, Huineng, shall move the Western Land for you, my Excellency, in a single kṣaṇa, so that it may be seen before your very eyes. Would you wish to see it?"
The Prefect prostrated himself and said:
"If I may behold it in this manner, what need is there to be reborn there?
I pray that the Venerable One, out of compassion, will manifest the Western Land for me; that would be most excellent!"
The Great Master said:
"Behold the West all at once!
When there is no longer doubt, you shall be liberated!"
The great assembly was struck with astonishment, not knowing what had occurred.
The Great Master said,
"Great assembly!..."
Great assembly!
Pay close attention and listen!
For worldly people, their own physical body is a city; the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are its gates.
Externally there are five gates; internally there is the gate of the mind.
The mind is the land, and its nature is the sovereign.
Where the nature is, the sovereign is; where the nature departs, the sovereign is gone.
When nature resides within body and mind, it exists; when nature departs, body and mind perish.
The Buddha is created by one's own nature; do not seek him outside the body.
When one's own nature is deluded, the Buddha is but a sentient being.
Awakening to one's own nature, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas. Compassion is Avalokiteśvara; joy and renunciation are named Śrīkṣetra (Potuozhi).

That which can purify is Śākyamuni; equanimity and rectitude are Maitreya. The self and others are Mount Sumeru; a deviant mind is the ocean water; afflictions are the waves; a poisonous mind is the evil dragon; worldly toil is the fish and turtles; falsehood is the ghosts and spirits; the three poisons are hell; ignorance is the animal realm; and the ten wholesome deeds are heaven.
When there is no self or person, Mount Sumeru collapses of its own accord;
when the deviant mind is eliminated, the ocean waters dry up;
when afflictions are absent, the waves subside.
Poisonous harms are eliminated, and fish and dragons cease to exist.

Within the ground of one’s own mind, the Tathāgata of awakened nature emits the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the six sense-gates until they are pure. This light shines through the various heavens of the six realms of desire; looking downward, it reaches the three poisons. Once these are removed, the hells are instantaneously extinguished. Inside and out, all is transparently clear, no different from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
"If one does not practice this cultivation, how can one reach that state?
When those in the assembly heard these words, their voices of praise reached the heavens; those who were deluded suddenly attained clear insight.
The Prefect prostrated himself and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“I universally pray that all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who hear this may simultaneously attain awakening and understanding.
The Great Master spoke for the thirty-sixth time:
“O Good Knowledge!”
If one wishes to practice cultivation, it can be accomplished at home as well as not necessarily in a monastery.
To reside in a monastery without practicing is like the people of the Western Regions who have evil hearts;
to practice while living at home is like the people of the Eastern Regions who cultivate goodness.
"I only wish that you cultivate purity within yourself; this itself is the Western Land.
The Magistrate asked, "Venerable Monk!"
"How should one practice while living as a householder?
We pray that you will instruct us.
The Great Master said:
“Good friends!

I, Huineng, have composed the ‘Verse on Formlessness’ for the sake of both monastics and laypeople. You should all recite it thoroughly; by practicing the teachings of the Sudden Dharma according to this verse, you will always be no different from me when we speak together.”
The verse says:
"The penetration of teaching and the penetration of mind are like the sun dwelling in the void;
transmitting only the teachings of the sudden [school], he transcends the world and shatters heterodox sects."
The teaching itself has neither sudden nor gradual aspects; it is only in delusion and awakening that there is slowness or speed.
If one studies the teachings of the sudden approach, the foolish cannot fully comprehend them.
Though the explanations may be of ten thousand kinds, when they accord with principle, they return to the One.
Within the dark house of afflictions, one must constantly give rise to the sun of wisdom.
When the false comes, it is due to afflictions; when the true comes, afflictions are eliminated.
When both the false and the true are no longer employed, one reaches pure clarity without remainder.
Awakening is fundamentally pure; to give rise to a thought is itself delusion.
Within this delusion, the nature of purity remains; one need only correctly eliminate the three obstructions.
If one cultivates the Way within the world, nothing whatsoever shall hinder it.
Constantly seeing one's own faults, one is immediately in accord with the Way.
Within the categories of form, the Way exists inherently;
to leave the Way and seek the Way elsewhere, seeking it without seeing it, leads only to regret in the end.
If you wish to seek the true Way, practicing rectitude is itself the Way;
if you yourself lack a correct mind, you will walk in darkness and not see the Way.
If one is a true cultivator of the Way, they do not perceive the faults of the world.
If you see the faults of the world, Your own faults are actually the opposite.
The faults of others are not my transgression; My own faults are my own transgression.
Simply eliminate the mind of fault-finding, And shatter the afflictions into pieces.
If one wishes to transform the ignorant, one must employ skillful means;
do not allow them to harbor doubt, for this is the manifestation of Bodhi.
The source of the Dharma exists within the world, both in the mundane and the supramundane.
Do not depart from the mundane world to seek the supramundane elsewhere.
False views reside within the mundane world, while right view is supramundane.
When both the false and the right are cast aside, the nature of bodhi remains vividly present.
"It is also called the Mahāyāna; though one has wandered through it for countless kalpas in delusion, awakening occurs in a single kṣaṇa.
Thus spoke the Great Master in the thirty-seventh chapter.
“Good friends!
You should all recite these verses and practice according to them; though you may be a thousand li away from Huineng, you will always be by his side.
If you do not practice according to them, though you face him, you will be a thousand li apart.”
Each person should cultivate for themselves; the Dharma does not depend on others.

The multitude shall now disperse, and I, Huineng, shall return to Mount Caoxi. If sentient beings have great doubts, come to that mountain and I will shatter your doubts so that we may together realize the Buddha-nature.
The officials and clergy present at the assembly prostrated themselves before the Upādhyāya, all of whom sighed in admiration, saying:
"How excellent is this great awakening! It is something we have never heard before. Southern China is truly blessed; a Buddha has been born here. Who could have known?"
At once, they all dispersed.
This was the thirty-eighth chapter. The Master went to Caoxi Mountain; he had practiced his teachings in the two prefectures of Shaozhou and Guangzhou for over forty years.
As for his disciples, whether monastics or laypeople, they number approximately three to five thousand, such that their names could not be fully recounted.
As for the essential tenets, he transmitted the *Platform Sutra* and took this as the basis for his teachings.
If one does not obtain the *Platform Sūtra*, there will be no formal transmission.
One must know the place of the Dharma, the year, month, day, and name by which it was successively entrusted from one to another.
Without the transmission of the *Platform Sutra*, one is not a disciple of the Southern School.
Those who have not received this transmission, though they may preach the teachings of sudden enlightenment, do not know its fundamental source and will ultimately fail to avoid contention.
Those who have attained the Dharma merely encourage the practice of cultivation; the mind that contends for victory or defeat is contrary to the Buddha-way.

Thirty-ninth: The people of this world all speak of the Southern School’s Neng and the Northern School’s Xiu, yet they do not know the fundamental facts of the matter. Furthermore, Master Xiu resided and practiced at Yuquan Temple in Dangyang County, Jingzhou, Jiangling Prefecture, in the Southern Capital, while Master Huineng resided and practiced at Caoxi Mountain, thirty-five li east of the city of Shaoguan.
The Dharma is but a single school; it is because people differ between North and South that the Northern and Southern schools were established.

As for the gradual and the sudden: the Dharma is but one kind, yet there are differences in the speed of realization. When realization is slow, it is called "gradual"; when realization is swift, it is called "sudden. The Dharma itself possesses neither gradual nor sudden aspects; rather, it is because people have sharp or dull faculties that the names "gradual" and "sudden" are applied.
In the fortieth chapter, Master Shenxiu often heard people say that Huineng’s Dharma was swift and pointed directly to the path of seeing.
Master Shenxiu then called his disciple, the monk Zhicheng, saying:
"You are clever and possess great wisdom. Go with me to Mount Caoxi to reach Huineng; pay your respects and listen carefully, but do not say that I sent you."
"Listen carefully to grasp the essential meaning, commit it to memory, and then come back and explain it to me. Let us see whose insight is sharper—mine or Huineng's.
You must come first; do not let me grow suspicious."

With sincere devotion, he accepted the mission and set out with joy. Within half a month, he arrived at Caoxi Mountain and saw Master Huineng; he prostrated himself and listened to the teachings, yet did not mention where he had come from.
Zhicheng heard the Dharma and attained awakening in that very instant; he immediately realized his original mind.
Rising at once, he prostrated and said, "O Preceptor!..."
"I, your disciple, came from Yuquan Temple; though I stayed with Master Xiu, I failed to attain awakening. Upon hearing the Venerable speak, I immediately realized my own original mind.
Out of your compassion, Venerable, I pray that you will instruct me."
Master Huineng said,
"Since you have come from there, must you not be a spy?
Zhi Cheng replied:
"No," said the Sixth Patriarch. "Why is it not so?"
Zhicheng said, "It is right when it has not yet been spoken; once it is spoken, it is no longer so.
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Afflictions are precisely bodhi; it is exactly like this!
The Great Master said to Zhicheng:

"I have heard that when you, Chan Master, teach people, you transmit only precepts, concentration, and wisdom (śīla-samādhi-prajñā). How does your Upādhyāya teach precepts, concentration, and wisdom to others?"
"You should explain this for me! Zhicheng said,
"Master Xiu spoke of precepts, concentration, and wisdom."

To refrain from all evil is called morality (*śīla*); to practice all that is good is called wisdom (*prajñā*); to purify one’s own mind is called concentration (*samādhi*). These are what are known as morality, concentration, and wisdom.
"He speaks in such a manner; I do not know what the Preceptor’s own view is.
Master Huineng replied, "This teaching is inconceivable, yet my own insight is different."
Zhicheng asked,
"How can they be distinguished? Huineng replied:
"I see that there are differences in speed.
With sincere resolve, he requested the Master to explain his insights regarding precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
The Great Master said:
"Listen to my words and observe what I see:

when the mind-ground is free from transgression, it is the self-nature precept; when the mind-ground is free from distraction, it is the self-nature concentration; when the mind-ground is free from delusion, it is the self-nature wisdom."
The Great Master said:
"Your teacher’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom are intended for those of small capacity and inferior intelligence;
my precepts, concentration, and wisdom are intended for those of superior intelligence."
"Having realized one's own nature, one likewise does not establish precepts, concentration, or wisdom.
Zhicheng said: "I request the Master to explain: how is it that they are not established?"
The Great Master said:

"Intrinsic nature is without fault, without confusion, and without delusion; with every thought-moment one contemplates through prajñā and remains constantly detached from the marks of dharmas—what, then, is there to be established?"
"Cultivating the self-nature instantaneously, there is no gradual progression; therefore, [stages] are not established.
Zhi Cheng prostrated himself and remained at Mount Caoxi, becoming a disciple and never leaving the Great Master's side.

The forty-second chapter: Furthermore, there was a monk named Fada who had constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for seven years, yet his mind remained deluded and he did not know the true essence of the Right Dharma.
He came to Caoxi Mountain to pay his respects and asked the Great Master, saying:

"I, your disciple, have constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for seven years, yet my mind remains confused and I do not know the true meaning of the Dharma. I have doubts regarding this sūtra; as the Great Master’s wisdom is vast and great, I pray that you will dispel these doubts."
The Great Master said:
"Fada! Your dharma is indeed thoroughly mastered, but your mind is not yet thoroughly mastered!"
"There is no doubt regarding the sutra; it is your own mind that is perverse as you seek the True Dharma. My mind is in right concentration, and this itself is the upholding of the sutra.
Throughout my entire life, I have not known written characters. Bring the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and read it to me once; upon hearing it, I shall immediately understand."

Fada took the sutra and arrived; he read it once before the Great Master. Having heard it, the Sixth Patriarch immediately understood the Buddha’s intent and then expounded the *Lotus Sutra* for Fada.
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Fada! The *Lotus Sutra* contains no many words; all seven fascicles are entirely composed of parables and causal conditions."
The Tathāgata extensively expounds the three vehicles solely because the faculties of worldly beings are dull.
The scriptural texts are clear: there are no other vehicles; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle.
The Great Master said:
"Fada! Listen to the Single Buddha Vehicle;
do not seek the Two Buddha Vehicles, for to be deluded is to obstruct your own nature."
In which part of the sutra is there the One Buddha Vehicle?
I shall explain it to you:
the sutra says, "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter."
The sixteen characters above constitute the True Dharma. How is this Dharma to be understood?
How is this Dharma to be cultivated?

Listen as I explain: when the human mind does not engage in discursive thought, its fundamental source is empty and quiescent; to depart from false views is itself the Great Matter of Cause and Condition.
To be undeluded regarding both the internal and the external is to depart from the two extremes.

To be deluded externally is to be attached to forms; to be deluded internally is to be attached to emptiness. To depart from form within form, and to depart from emptiness within emptiness, is precisely what it means to be undeluded.
If one awakens to this Dharma, the mind opens in a single thought-moment and appears in the world.
What is it that opens? It is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"Buddha" is synonymous with "Awakening," which is divided into four gates:
awakening to insight and knowledge, demonstrating insight and knowledge, realizing insight and knowledge, and entering into insight and knowledge.

This is called opening, revealing, awakening, and entering. Entering through a single point, one immediately awakens to and perceives it; seeing one's own original nature, one immediately attains transcendence of the world.
The Great Master said:
"Fada! I always wish that all people in the world would constantly open their own minds to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, rather than opening the knowledge and vision of sentient beings."
When the minds of worldly people are deviant, they create evil through delusion and ignorance, thereby opening up the cognitive perspectives of sentient beings;
when the minds of worldly people are upright, they give rise to wisdom and contemplative observation, thereby opening up the cognitive perspectives of the Buddha.
"Do not open the knowledge and vision of sentient beings; opening the knowledge and vision of the Buddha is what constitutes transcending the world.
The Great Master said, "Fada!
This is the One Vehicle Dharma of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
It is divided into three below for the sake of those who are deluded.
You should simply rely upon the Single Buddha Vehicle.
The Great Master said:
“Fada! Let the mind-practice revolve the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; do not let the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* revolve you.”
When the mind is upright, one turns the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; when the mind is deviant, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* turns one.
To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is to turn the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; to open the knowledge and vision of sentient beings is to be turned by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Great Master said, "To diligently practice according to the Dharma is itself to turn the sutra.
Upon hearing this, Fahada attained great enlightenment beneath the words; weeping and sobbing with grief, he addressed him, saying:
“Upādhyāya! Truly, I have never turned the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; for seven years, I was turned by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Since then, I have turned the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, practicing the conduct of the Buddha in every thought-moment.”
The Great Master said,
"It is precisely the Buddha’s practice that is the Buddha.
At that time, among those who heard him, there was not one who did not attain awakening.
In the forty-third chapter, there was a monk named Zhichang who came to Caoxi Mountain to pay his respects to the Master and inquire about the principles of the Fourfold Dharma.
Zhichang asked the Master, saying:
"The Buddha spoke of the Three Vehicles, yet also spoke of the Supreme Vehicle. Your disciple does not understand this; I hope you will instruct me."
Master Huineng said: "You should see with your own mind;
do not cling to external phenomena. Originally, there are no four vehicles of the Dharma.
It is because the human mind’s capacity is fourfold that the Dharma appears as four vehicles."
To see, hear, read, and recite is the Small Vehicle; to awaken to the Dharma and understand its meaning is the Middle Vehicle; to practice in accordance with the Dharma is the Great Vehicle.

When all phenomena are fully understood and all practices are complete, when nothing is abandoned yet one merely leaves behind the marks of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and acts without attainment, this is the Supreme Vehicle. The Supreme Vehicle is the meaning of the "highest practice"; it does not reside in verbal disputes. You must cultivate it yourself; do not ask me about it.
In the forty-fourth section, there was also a monk named Shenhui, a native of Xiangyang.
He went to Caoxi Mountain to pay his respects and asked,
"When you practice seated meditation, Master, do you see or not?"
The Great Master rose and struck Shenhui three times, then asked Shenhui,
"When I strike you, does it hurt or not?
Shenhui replied:
"Neither painful nor not painful," the Sixth Patriarch said,
"I also see and I also do not see."
Shenhui asked again:
"Why does the Great Master both see and not see?
The Great Master said:
"I also see" means that I constantly observe my own faults and afflictions; therefore, it is said that "I also see.
"I also do not see" means that I do not observe the faults or transgressions of others; thus, it is "also seeing and also not seeing."
"Are you in pain, or are you not in pain? Shenhui replied,
"If I were not in pain, I would be the same as insentient wood and stone."
"If you feel pain, you are the same as ordinary people, and you will immediately give rise to resentment.
The Master said, "Shenhui!..."
Move forward!
To see or not to see are two extremes; to feel pain or not to feel pain are birth and cessation.
You have not yet even seen your own nature—how dare you come here to deceive others?
Shenhui prostrated himself, prostrated again, and remained silent.
The Master said:
"Your mind is deluded and you do not see; go ask a Good Friend (Kalyāṇamitra) to find the way."
Your mind has awakened and you have seen for yourself; practice according to the Dharma.
You were deluded yourself and did not see your own mind, yet you come here to ask whether Huineng can see it?
I do not know it myself; I cannot substitute for your delusion.
"If you could see for yourself, would you not have dispelled my delusion?
Why do you not cultivate for yourself instead of asking me whether I see?
Shenhui prostrated himself and became a disciple, never leaving Mount Caoshi and always remaining by his side.
In the forty-fifth chapter, the Great Master then summoned his disciples: Fahai, Zhicheng, Fada, Zhichang, Zhitong, Zhiche, Zhidao, Fazhen, Faru, and Shenhui.
The Great Master said:
"You ten disciples, come forward. You are not like the others; after my parinirvāṇa, each of you shall be a teacher for one quarter of the world."
I teach you how to expound the Dharma so as not to lose its fundamental principle.

I present the dharma-gate of the three categories and employ the thirty-six pairs; appearing and disappearing, yet remaining detached from both extremes, you must, in expounding all dharmas, never depart from their essential nature and characteristics.

If someone asks about the Dharma, every word spoken is dualistic, taking up phenomena as its counterparts; coming and going are mutually dependent, yet ultimately these two phenomena are both eliminated, leaving no further place to go.
The three categories of the Dharma-gate are the aggregates (skandha), the elements (dhātu), and the bases (āyatana).
The aggregates refer to the five aggregates;
the elements refer to the eighteen elements.
The "entrances" (āyatana) refer to these twelve entrances.
What are called the five aggregates (skandha)?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
What are called the eighteen elements (dhātus)?
They are the six objects, the six sense-gates, and the six consciousnesses.
What are called the twelve bases (āyatanas)?
The six external objects and the six internal gates.
What are called the six objects?
They are form, sound, fragrance, flavor, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
What are called the six gates?
They are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
From the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the six consciousnesses arise.
