Visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness—these are the six gates and the six objects.
Because its self-nature contains all phenomena, it is called the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness).

Discursive thought is the evolving consciousness; it gives rise to the six consciousnesses, which emerge through the six gates and engage with the six objects—these constitute three times six, or eighteen.
Due to the perversion of their own nature, they give rise to the eighteen perversions;
if their own nature were correct, they would give rise to the eighteen correctnesses.
When used adversely, it is sentient beings; when used skillfully, it is the Buddha.
By what is this usage determined?
It is determined by self-nature (*svabhāva*).
The Forty-sixth Chapter: "Oppositions.
There are five types of opposition between external, insentient objects:
heaven and earth oppose each other; the sun and moon oppose each other; darkness and light oppose each other; yin and yang oppose each other; and water and fire oppose each other.
The principles of linguistic expression involve twelve pairs of opposites:

the pair of the conditioned and the unconditioned; the pair of the material and the immaterial; the pair of the characterized and the uncharacterized; the pair of the tainted and the untainted; the pair of form and emptiness; the pair of movement and stillness; the pair of clarity and turbidity; the pair of the ordinary and the sagely; the pair of the monastic and the lay; the pair of old and young; the pair of long and short; and the pair of high and low.
There are nineteen pairs of the arising of function from self-nature:

the pair of the heterodox and the orthodox; delusion and wisdom; folly and knowledge; distraction and concentration; precepts and their opposite; rectitude and crookedness; reality and falsehood; the precipitous and the level; afflictions and bodhi; kindness and harm; joy and anger; equanimity and stinginess; progress and retreat; birth and extinction; permanence and impermanence; the dharma-body and the form-body; the transformation-body and the reward-body; essence and function; and nature and phenomena.

There are twelve pairs of opposites concerning language and phenomena, five pairs of opposites concerning external objects and insentient things, and nineteen pairs of opposites concerning the arising of function from self-nature; these together constitute thirty-six pairs.
These thirty-six pairs of dharmas provide a method of understanding that applies to all sutras; they involve entering and emerging from both extremes of existence and non-existence.
How do these thirty-six pairs function as the arising of self-nature in common speech with others?
When going out, one dwells in the signless within signs;
when entering within, one dwells in emptiness within emptiness.
To be attached to emptiness merely prolongs ignorance.
To cling to signs is merely to perpetuate false views.
To uphold the Dharma with direct speech is to not rely on written words.
Since it is said that one does not rely on written words?
A person should not engage in speech, for speech is itself mere characters.
While one speaks of emptiness from the standpoint of self-nature, the very nature of speech itself is not empty.
It is because of delusion regarding one's own nature that speech must be eliminated.
Darkness is not dark by itself; it is dark because of light.
Darkness is not dark by itself; it becomes dark because of light.
It is through darkness that light is manifested; their coming and going are mutually dependent. The thirty-six pairs are likewise thus.
The Great Master spoke as follows:
"My ten disciples!
From now on, in the transmission of the Dharma, you shall successively instruct one another using this single scroll of the *Platform Sūtra*, so that you do not lose the fundamental school."
Not to receive and uphold the *Platform Sūtra* is not my school’s fundamental tenet.
Now that you have obtained it, let it be transmitted and circulated from generation to generation.
Those who encounter the *Platform Sūtra* are as if seeing me personally bestowing it upon them.

After the ten monks had received the instructions, they transcribed them as the *Platform Sutra*, which has been transmitted from generation to generation; those who obtain it will surely realize their own nature.
On the third day of the eighth month in the second year of the Xuantian era, the Great Master entered nirvana at the age of forty-eight.
On the eighth day of the seventh month, he summoned his disciples to bid them farewell.

The Great Master had constructed a stupa at Guoen Temple in Xinzhou during the first year of the Xiantian era; on the eighth day of the seventh month of the second year of Xiantian, he announced his departure.
The Great Master said:

"You assembly, draw near; in the eighth month I shall depart from this world. If you have any doubts, ask them soon so that I may shatter your uncertainties, cause those who are deluded to attain full awakening, and bring you peace and happiness."
"If I depart, there will be no one left to instruct you.
When the assembly of monks, including Fahai, heard this, they wept with tears and lamented in sorrow.
Only Shenhui remained unmoved, neither weeping nor lamenting.
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"The young monk Shenhui, however, has attained equanimity toward the good and the not-good, remaining unmoved by blame or praise.
As for the others, they have not attained this; having been in the mountains for several years, what further path have they cultivated?"
As you weep now in sorrow, for whom else do you grieve?
Do you grieve because I do not know where I am going?
If I did not know my destination, I would never have parted from you.
Because you weep with grief, you do not know my place of departure;
if you knew my place of departure, you would not weep with grief.
The essential nature of reality is without birth or extinction, and without going or coming.
"All of you, sit down; I shall give you a verse:
'The Verse on the Real and the False, the Active and the Still. All of you should memorize it, for by seeing the meaning of this verse, you will find it to be identical with my own intention."
"By practicing in accordance with this, you will not lose the fundamental purpose.
The assembly prostrated and requested the Great Master to leave behind a verse, which they respectfully received and upheld.
The verse says:
"All things lack reality; one does not perceive reality through perception.
If one perceives reality, that perception itself is entirely unreal.
If one can possess reality within oneself, then by departing from the false, the mind is true."
One's own mind does not depart from the provisional; if there is no reality, where could reality be found?
That which has sentience is characterized by movement; that which lacks sentience is without movement.
If you cultivate a practice of non-movement, you will be the same as the insentient, which is unmoving.
If one perceives true immovability, there is immovability within movement;
this immovability is itself immovable, yet it is devoid of insentient matter and lacks the seeds of Buddhahood.
One who can skillfully discern these characteristics abides in the immovability of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If you awaken to this seeing, it is the functioning of True Suchness (Tathatā).
I inform all those who study the Way: you must strive and apply your minds with diligence.
Do not, within the gateway of the Mahāyāna, instead cling to the wisdom of birth and death.
If one finds that another is in accord with oneself, one should immediately discuss the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching together.
If they are truly not in accord, one should join one's palms, pay respects, and encourage them toward goodness.
This teaching is fundamentally without contention; if one contends, one loses the intent of the Way.
"Those who cling to the methods of dispute / Enter birth and death by their very nature.
(49) Upon hearing this, the assembly of monks understood the Great Master’s intent; they no longer dared to dispute and practiced according to the Dharma.
Having prostrated once, he immediately knew that the Great Master would not remain in this world for long.
The Elder Fahai stepped forward and said,
"Great Master!..."
"After the Great Master has departed, to whom should the robe and the Dharma be entrusted?
The Great Master said, "The Dharma has already been entrusted; you need not ask."
"More than twenty years after my parinirvāṇa, heterodox teachings will arise in confusion, deluding the core tenets of my school.
Should someone emerge who, disregarding their own life, definitively establishes the right and wrong of the Buddha-dharma and upholds its core tenets, that shall be my true Dharma."

The transmission of the robe is not appropriate; if you do not believe me, I shall recite for you the "Verses on the Transmission of the Robe and the Entrustment of the Dharma" by the Five Patriarchs of former times.
According to the intent of the first patriarch, Bodhidharma’s verse, it is not appropriate to transmit the robe.
"Listen as I recite with you. He chanted:
"The First Patriarch, Venerable Bodhidharma, chanted: [Verse follows]"
"I originally came from the Eastern Land, To transmit the Teaching and save deluded hearts;
One flower blooms and five petals unfold, The fruit ripens of its own accord.
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Huìkě, spoke this verse:
"Originally there was ground due to conditions; from the ground, seeds gave rise to flowers.
When, in the ultimate sense, there was originally no ground, from where could the flowers have arisen?
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, offered this verse:
"Flower seeds require the earth; Planted upon the earth, flowers grow.
Yet flower seeds have no nature of arising, And within the earth, there is likewise no arising.
The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, spoke this verse:
"The seed of a flower possesses the nature of arising; Depending on the ground, it produces flowers.
If the prior conditions do not harmonize, Nothing at all will arise.
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, spoke this verse:
“When sentient beings come to sow seeds, Non-sentient things immediately produce flowers.
Since non-sentient things have no seeds, The mind-ground likewise has no birth.
The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Huineng, spoke this verse:
“When the ground of the mind contains the seeds of emotion, the rain of Dharma causes flowers to bloom immediately.
Once one awakens to these flower-seeds of emotion, the fruit of Bodhi is naturally attained.
Thus spoke Master Neng in the fiftieth chapter.
"Listen as I compose two verses for you, capturing the essential meaning of Master Dharma’s verses.
You deluded ones, if you rely on these verses in your practice, you will surely realize your nature."
The first verse says:
"The perverse flowers bloom upon the ground of the mind; The five petals follow along with the root.
Together they create the karma of ignorance, And the view is blown away by the wind of karma."
The second verse says:
"When the true flower blooms upon the ground of the mind, / Five petals follow along with the root.
/ Together cultivating the wisdom of prajñā, / One shall attain the Buddha’s bodhi in the future."
After the Sixth Patriarch had finished reciting the verse, he dismissed the assembly.
His disciples went outside and reflected, realizing that the Great Master would not remain in this world for long.
Chapter Fifty-One: After the Sixth Patriarch’s passing, on the third day of the eighth month, following the midday meal, the Great Master said:
"Take your seats; I shall now part from you!
Fahai asked, "As for this transmission of the Sudden Teaching, how many generations have passed from the beginning until the present?"
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Originally, the transmission was passed down through the Seven Buddhas;
Śākyamuni Buddha was the seventh, Mahākāśyapa the eighth, Ānanda the ninth, Madhyāntika the tenth, and Śāṇakavāsin the eleventh."
Upagupta was the twelfth; Tiṣya was the thirteenth; Buddhanandi was the fourteenth;
Buddhamitra was the fifteenth; Pārśva Bhikṣu was the sixteenth;
Puṇyayaśas was the seventeenth; Aśvaghoṣa was the eighteenth; and the Elder Vīra was the nineteenth.
Nāgārjuna was the twentieth; Kāṇadeva was the twenty-first; Rāhula was the twenty-second;
Saṃghanandi was the twenty-third; Saṃghayaśas was the twenty-fourth;
Kumārabuddhi was the twenty-fifth; Jayata was the twenty-sixth; and Vasu...
Paṇḍa, the twenty-seventh; Maṇḍara, the twenty-eighth;
Hakkula, the twenty-ninth; Siṃhabhikṣu, the thirtieth;
Śāṇavāsa, the thirty-first; Upāhu, the thirty-second; Saṃghala, the thirty-third; Subhamitra.
Thirty-fourth, Prince Bodhidharma, third son of the King of South India;
thirty-fifth, the monk Huìkè of the Tang state; thirty-sixth, Sēngcàn; thirty-seventh, Dàoxìn;
thirty-eighth, Hóngrěn; thirty-ninth, Huìnéng himself, who is contemporary with the present day.
"The Forty-first Dharma of Receiving.
The Great Master said:
"From this day forward, as you transmit these teachings to one another in succession, there must be strict adherence to the instructions; do not lose the fundamental principle."
The fifty-second, Zhe Fahai, again addressed him, saying:
"Master, as you now depart, what Dharma do you leave behind? How shall those of future generations perceive the Buddha?"
The Sixth Patriarch said: "Listen!
Those deluded people of future generations will realize that by simply recognizing sentient beings, they can see the Buddha."
If you do not recognize sentient beings, you will not be able to see the Buddha even after ten thousand kalpas.

I now instruct you to recognize sentient beings so that you may see the Buddha; I further leave behind this "Verses on Liberation through Seeing the True Buddha. If you are deluded, you will not see the Buddha; if you awaken, you shall see him immediately.
“Dharma Ocean, I wish for you to hear this so that it may be transmitted from generation to generation and continue unceasingly through every lifetime.
The Sixth Patriarch said: “Listen!”
I shall explain this to you:

if people of future generations wish to seek the Buddha, they need only recognize sentient beings, and they will thereby recognize the Buddha. It is because of the mind of the Buddha that there are sentient beings; apart from sentient beings, there is no mind of the Buddha.
Delusion is the sentient being as Buddha; awakening is the sentient being as Buddha.
Ignorance is the Buddha as sentient being; wisdom is the sentient being as Buddha.
The treacherous mind is the Buddha as sentient being; equanimity is the sentient being as Buddha.
If the mind throughout one’s life is treacherous, the Buddha dwells among sentient beings.
If in a single thought it awakens to being level, then sentient beings are themselves the Buddha.
Within my own mind there is a Buddha; this self-Buddha is the true Buddha.
"If you yourselves lack the Buddha-mind, where else would you go to seek the Buddha?
The Great Master said in the fifty-third chapter:
"My disciples, dwell well!"
I leave behind one verse, titled "The Verse on Seeing the True Buddha through One's Own Nature and Attaining Liberation.
When those deluded by later generations hear the meaning of this verse, they will immediately perceive the true Buddha within their own mind and own nature.
"I give you this verse as my parting gift from you.
The verse says:
"The pure nature of True Suchness is the true Buddha; Wrong views and the three poisons are the true Māra."
Where a person of wrong views dwells, Māra resides in their house; where a person of right views dwells, the Buddha resides in their hall.
When wrong views arise within one's nature, the three poisons are born; this is precisely when the King of Māras comes to dwell in one's house.
When right view suddenly eliminates the three poisons of the mind, the Māra is transformed into a Buddha—truly without artifice.
The transformation body, the reward body, and the dharma body: these three bodies are fundamentally one body.
If one seeks self-seeing within the fundamental nature, this is precisely the cause for attaining the Bodhi of Buddhahood.
Originally, the pure nature arises from the transformation body; the pure nature is ever-present within the transformation body.
The nature causes the emanation-body to practice the Right Path; in the future, it will be perfectly fulfilled and truly inexhaustible.
The nature of lust is itself the cause of the pure nature; were lust removed, there would be no body of pure nature.
Within the nature itself, simply remain free from the five desires; seeing the nature in a single instant is itself the truth.
If in this life one awakens to the gate of the sudden teaching, awakening is to see the World-Honored One before one’s very eyes.
If you wish to practice and seek to find the Buddha, yet do not know where to seek the Truth,
if you can possess the Truth within your own mind, that very Truth is the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Not seeking the Truth for oneself but looking for the Buddha elsewhere— To go in search of it is nothing but a great deluded person.
The Dharma of the Sudden Teaching flows from the West; To save and deliver the world, one must cultivate oneself.
"Now I respond to those in the world who study the Way: if you do not rely on this, you will remain in great indolence.
Having finished speaking these verses, the Great Master addressed his disciples, saying:

"Stay well. I now part from you; after I have gone, do not act out of worldly sentiment by weeping, accepting condolences and money or silk, or wearing mourning clothes. These are not the Holy Dharma, nor are you my disciples."

Just as when I was in the world, there was a certain kind of person who, sitting upright at one time, remained simply without movement or stillness, without arising or ceasing, without going or coming, without right or wrong, and without abiding—serene and tranquil; this is precisely the Great Way.
"After I have departed, you should simply practice according to the Dharma, just as you did while I was alive;
for if I were still in the world and you were to violate the teachings, my remaining would be of no benefit."
After the Great Master had spoken these words, at the third watch of the night, he suddenly passed away.
The Master was seventy-six years of age.
On the day of the Great Master’s parinirvāṇa, the fifty-fourth [year], a wondrous fragrance permeated the temple, lingering for several days without dispersing.
Mountains collapsed and the earth shook; the forests turned white, and the sun and moon lost their radiance while the wind and clouds faded in color.

On the third day of the eighth month, he passed into *nirvāṇa*. When his honored seat was brought to Caoxi Mountain on the eleventh month for burial within Longkan, a white light appeared, surging straight up to the heavens, only dispersing after three days.
Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaoyang, erected a stele for it, which has been venerated until the present day.
This is the fifty-fifth folding of the *Platform Sutra*, compiled by the Venerable Fahai.
The Elder passed away and entrusted [the lineage] to his fellow student Daoji.
Daoji passed away and entrusted it to his disciple Wuzhen.
Wuzhen resided at Faxing Monastery on Mount Caoxi in Lingnan, where he currently transmits this Dharma.

Fifty-sixth Chapter: Entrusting This Dharma. To receive this dharma, one must possess superior faculties and wisdom, have deep faith in the Buddha-dharma, and establish oneself in great compassion; thus upholding this sutra as a lineage of transmission that remains uninterrupted to this day.
The fifty-seventh, Master Zhe, was originally a native of Qujiang County in Shaoyang Prefecture.
When the Tathāgata entered nirvana and the Dharma teachings flowed eastward to this land, he together with others transmitted the mind of non-abiding—that is, my own mind is non-abiding.
This is the teaching spoken by true Bodhisattvas, consisting of both the ultimate truth and its analogies; it instructs only those of great wisdom, for non-abiding is the foundation of this intent.

Only to those who have made vows to practice, who do not retreat when encountering difficulties during their cultivation, who are able to endure suffering, and whose merit and virtue are profound, should this Dharma be bestowed.

If a person’s faculties and nature are inadequate, such that they cannot grasp the measure [of the teaching], and although they seek this Dharma, they cannot establish it, one must not recklessly entrust them with the *Platform Sūtra*.
I address all my fellow practitioners, so that they may understand this esoteric intent.
